name: North Ridge
approach: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.

itinerary.cal: The ridge and the slopes above the tarn can hold snow into early summer; most parties climb it July-October.

days.note: About 10 miles of up-and-down trail up the Wolf Creek valley, through forest burned in 2021, to the meadows at the end of the Wolf Creek Trail. The trail drops a couple of hundred feet right after the trailhead, which has to be regained at the very end of the trip.
days.title: Hike Wolf Creek to Gardner Meadows

schedule.label: Camp at Gardner Meadows
schedule.detail: Established sites near the end of the trail; more flat spots in the trees by the creek.

days.objective: Reach camp at Gardner Meadows

days.note: Cross Wolf Creek from the last campsites and follow a faint path that soon fades into old burn. Keep high above Abernathy Lake and traverse up into the upper basin with the small tarn and the remains of a mining camp. Climb the spur ridge from the tarn to the main north ridge (a few exposed class 3 moves), follow a short boot path past old mining debris on the crest, then scramble class 2-3 boulders and scree to the summit. Descend by the scree slope or the old path back to the tarn, return to camp and either hike out or spend a second night.
days.title: North ridge scramble, then out

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Cross Wolf Creek and head for the upper tarn, staying above Abernathy Lake.

schedule.label: Spur ridge to the north ridge
schedule.detail: A few exposed class 3 moves; then a short boot path past old mining debris.

schedule.label: Summit (8,321 ft)
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 boulders and scree along the crest.

schedule.label: Back to camp
schedule.detail: Scree slope or the old path down to the tarn; then retrace the line to Gardner Meadows.

days.objective: Summit via the tarn, the spur ridge and the north ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A remote trip, usually done with a night at Gardner Meadows: about 10 miles of trail each way, then an off-trail climb from the meadows to the summit and back.

name: Diobsud Creek Glacier
approach: Drive Baker Lake Road (FR-11) to FR-1106, then FR-1107 to its end at the Watson Lakes Trailhead (~4,360 ft, Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary nearby). Start on the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail (Trail #611), which climbs gently through forest for about 1 mile to a junction with the Anderson Butte Trail (#611.1); stay left/straight on #611. Continue about another half mile to a second junction, about 1.5 miles from the trailhead — the right fork drops 0.5 mile to Lower Anderson Lake, while the climber's route bears left and climbs to a ridge saddle (~600 ft above the trailhead) where the trail crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping toward the Watson Lakes. From this saddle, leave the maintained tread and pick up a boot path heading south along the ridge, staying high above Lower Anderson Lake, through meadows to Upper Anderson Lake (~5,100-5,300 ft) — the last easy, reliable water before things get rougher. From Upper Anderson Lake, angle northeast up a short wooded gully, then continue across open rock slabs, scree, and lingering snowfields on Mt. Watson's north side, crossing another saddle near 5,300 ft before descending through heather to the Diobsud Lakes basin (figure roughly 5-6 hours car-to-lakes for a fit party) — the last dependable camp/water source below the peak. From Diobsud Lakes the route turns unpleasant: sidehilling across slippery vegetation, brush and cedar thickets, mossy slab scrambling, and steep dirt/scree gullies with real loose-rock hazard lead up onto Bacon's south ridge. Once on the south ridge, broad snow slopes lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier. Rope up here — the glacier holds real crevasse hazard (parties report needing to probe, especially early and late season, though the upper apron is sometimes reported clean in a good snow year) — and climb/traverse northwest toward the col below the summit pyramid (roughly 6,200-6,300 ft), finishing on broad summit snow slopes to a short summit arête. Snow condition (firm morning snow vs. slushy afternoon) matters a lot on both the gully and glacier sections, so an early start is standard. The gully leading from Diobsud Lakes basin up to the south ridge/glacier access can be avalanche-prone in snow-covered conditions.
descent: Reverse the glacier and approach; rope up for the icecap.

bivy.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
bivy.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward Berdeen, or for the long line north over the divide toward Hagan and Blum. What sets it apart from every other high site here is that it has water at six thousand feet, which nothing on the connecting ridges does. It is alpine meadow, so the heather is the thing to protect and the tent goes on rock. Snow covers this basin well into July and the lakes can still be part frozen at the start of the season. There is no shelter, no cell coverage, and no quick way down from here in any direction.
bivy.water: The lakes, dependable and right at camp — the best water this high anywhere on the massif. Treat it.
bivy.permit: This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required for an overnight, collected in person at the wilderness information center. No campfires. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste in a blue bag from snow and glacier ground. The party limit in a park cross-country zone is small — confirm the number when you collect the permit rather than assuming a Forest Service twelve.
bivy.capacity: Room for a small party or two on alpine meadow and heather benches beside the upper pair of lakes; established by use rather than designation, with no facilities

bivy.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. The road is the problem: FS 1107 has been closed at a washout at milepost 3.8, well below the road end, since July 8, 2026, and the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert, still posted on September 26, 2026, gives no end date; the closure cuts off the trailhead and the Anderson Creek Sno-Park. While it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because Bacon Peak's approach runs directly above it. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. Camping is allowed only in the designated sites and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
bivy.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. From camp the summit is a short ascent to the southeast, and it is possible to reach the top without crossing glaciers at all, which is what makes this a scramble for a competent party rather than a rope-up. Immediately north the ground falls away past post-glacial moraine to the saddle above the green lake below the glacier, and that is the line onward for anyone continuing east or north across the range. It is a fully exposed shelf with nothing to shelter behind and the weather here comes across from Baker with no warning. The season is roughly mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse is a long snow slope, later and the water is gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier melt near camp through most of the season, and tarns in the moraine below. Late in a dry summer expect to be melting snow. Treat anything you find, and do not count on liquid water in early season when the whole shelf is still covered.
bivy.permit: This camp sits on the boundary country between the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness and North Cascades National Park, and which one it falls in decides whether you need a permit at all. Ask specifically when you plan the trip: the Forest Service side needs no overnight permit, while the park side needs a backcountry permit written for the correct cross-country zone. No campfires on either side of the line. Camp on snow, rock or gravel and never on the heather, keep well back from water, and pack out all waste — on snow and glacier that means blue bags carried out.
bivy.capacity: Open ground for a couple of small parties on gravel, rock and heather about half a mile northeast of the summit; informal, with nothing built and no toilet

itinerary.cal: Usually two or three days from the Watson Lakes trailhead.

days.note: hike to the saddle, take the ridge path to Upper Anderson Lake, then cross the slabs, scree and snowfields on Mt. Watson's north side and over the 5,300 ft saddle, dropping through heather to camp at the Diobsud Lakes, about 6 hours for a fit party.

sidehill and climb the loose gullies to Bacon's south ridge, rope up on the Diobsud Creek Glacier and climb to the summit, about 6 hours from the lakes, then return to camp (or carry over and camp at the 6,250 ft saddle below the summit).
reverse the traverse to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Access gully to Diobsud Creek Glacier

name: Twin Sisters Olivine Scramble
approach: Start at the Elbow Lake Trailhead (USFS Trail #697), at the end of FS Road 38 (the Mosquito Lake Road / FS-38 drive from Deming/Acme). The trail immediately meets the Middle Fork Nooksack River — there is no bridge at the marked crossing, and fording can be dangerous or outright impassable during high water; many parties instead use an unofficial log crossing roughly 1/4 mile downstream from the official ford, made of logs lashed between two boulders. Once across, pick up the Elbow Lake Trail proper and climb through forest for about 1.5 miles to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where an unmaintained but well-trodden, blue-blazed 'Green Creek Climber's Trail' splits off to the left into the Green Creek cirque (look closely for the small blue markers — it's easy to walk past). Follow this climber's trail up into the basin; Green Creek itself runs clear and is a reliable water source along this stretch. Above treeline the trail gives way to talus and boulder fields and then loose, unstable scree, with class 3 rock steps required to reach the toe of the Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier — route-finding through this section is the crux of the approach, and parties should expect to hunt for the least-loose line. Cross the low-angle glacier (crevasse hazard is generally low here but rises later season; carry basic glacier gear) up to the low notch on the ridge between Cinderella and Little Sister, which is the jumping-off point for Cinderella's west ridge/north face. Elevation gain from the river crossing to this notch is substantial — roughly 4,000 ft over about five miles — and fit parties often go car-to-car in one long day, while others split it with a camp in the Green Creek basin.

bivy.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
bivy.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
bivy.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
bivy.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
bivy.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

itinerary.cal: The Middle Fork Nooksack bridge/log crossing at the start of the Elbow Lake Trail washes out periodically - check recent trip reports before relying on a dry crossing.

days.note: Walk or bike the 4 closed miles of FR 38 from the washout to the Elbow Lake trailhead first. Fit parties often do this as one long car-to-car day; others camp in the Green Creek basin. While FS Road 38 is closed by its washout, biking the closed road miles saves the legs. From the trailhead, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack, hike the Elbow Lake Trail through old growth to the Hildebrand Creek switchback, and follow the blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' trail into the cirque, across the low-angle glacier to the Cinderella-Little Sister notch and up the west ridge on grippy olivine rock to the summit. Descend by reversing the route, including re-biking the closed road miles at the end.
days.title: Bike/hike approach and ridge scramble to the summit

schedule.label: Leave car, bike the logging road
schedule.detail: FS Road 38 is closed by a washout at milepost 7, about 4 miles short of the trailhead; biking those closed miles saves time and legs.

schedule.label: Stash bikes, start Elbow Lake Trail on foot
schedule.detail: Cross the Middle Fork Nooksack right at the trailhead (no bridge), then climb through old growth above the Green Creek valley about 1.5 mi to the Hildebrand Creek switchback, where the blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' trail branches off.

schedule.label: Reach the Green Creek cirque
schedule.detail: Talus, loose scree and Class 3 rock steps lead to the toe of the glacier; cross it to the notch between Cinderella and Little Sister.

schedule.label: Ridge/gully scramble to Cinderella summit
schedule.detail: Class 3-4 scrambling on solid, high-friction olivine rock; some exposed ridge sections and route-finding around gendarmes.

schedule.label: Reverse the scramble and hike back to bikes
schedule.detail: Downclimb the ridge, retrace the glacier, the Green Creek climbers' trail and the Elbow Lake Trail.

schedule.label: Bike out to the car
schedule.detail: Mostly downhill/flat closed-road miles back to the vehicle.

days.objective: Summit Cinderella Peak via the west ridge olivine scramble, car-to-car

itinerary.totalNote: A long single push: roughly 11-12 hours car-to-car, ~12 miles and ~5,400 ft of gain, done in a day, as many fit parties do.

waypoints.name: Twin Sisters Viewpoint / Green Creek climbers' trail split

name: South Route
approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead drop about 200-250' off the ridge crest into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile cross-country (talus, slabs, occasional snow) staying near 5,800', to a camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050' near two streams fed by overhead slabs (reliable water, unlike the Barrier). From this basin camp, descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col and onto the route involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty (this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light) before reaching the col, from which the route climbs East Twin Needle's summit block directly above.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb and make short rappels down the south gullies to the Eye Col, then descend into Crescent Creek Basin.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the south side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the separate Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry permit for Terror/Crescent Creek Basin camps, and the Barrier is normally only safely crossable July-September once seasonal snow bridges and the approach brush have opened up.

days.note: A grueling cross-country day: old roadbed and steep, brushy boot path from Goodell Creek Trailhead past Terror Creek, then a loose, exposed scramble across the Barrier into the Crescent Creek Basin drainage. Most parties camp on a flat bench or col around 6,000-6,400 ft, close under the Chopping Block/Twin Needles group.
days.title: Approach over the Barrier to high camp

schedule.label: Leave Goodell Creek Trailhead
schedule.detail: Follow the old logging roadbed roughly 4 miles before it fades into boot-path.

schedule.label: Ford Terror Creek, start steep climber's path
schedule.detail: Very steep, root- and brush-choked trail gaining toward treeline.

schedule.label: Cross the Barrier
schedule.detail: Loose, exposed ledges and talus at ~6,000-6,400 ft; the crux of the approach and route-finding.

schedule.label: Arrive high camp
schedule.detail: Camp near the Chopping Block col or on benches above Crescent Creek Basin.

days.objective: Reach camp in/above Crescent Creek Basin

days.note: An alpine-start day from camp: cross Crescent Creek Basin's snow and talus to Eye Col, the notch between the two Twin Needles, then scramble/climb the South Route to East Twin Needle's summit. Most parties use the same col to tack on West Twin Needle's easier class 2-3 west slope before returning to camp.
days.title: East (and West) Twin Needle via Eye Col

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start to cross snow/talus in basin while firm.

schedule.label: Gain Eye Col
schedule.detail: Loose gully between the two Needles: small chockstones low down are scrambled, the bigger ones higher up are fifth class and usually pitched out, then a short scree walk to the col.

schedule.label: South Route to East Twin Needle summit
schedule.detail: Steep rock on the summit block directly above the col, with a short hand-crack crux near the top; parties rope up.

schedule.label: Descend to Eye Col, tag West Twin Needle
schedule.detail: Optional: easier class 2-3 west slope from the col if time and weather allow.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Reverse gullies/rappels down to Crescent Creek Basin and camp.

days.objective: Summit East Twin Needle, tag West Twin Needle if conditions allow

name: Sitkum Glacier
approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (off Sloan Creek Road, FR 49), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Red Creek bridge to Mackinaw Shelter, then up a long series of switchbacks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly 8-9 miles from the car. White Pass and its camp are a short way south along the PCT; this route does not go there. Turn north on the PCT and cross Red Pass (about 6,500 ft) a mile or two on, then descend into the upper White Chuck valley and follow the PCT down it for roughly 7-9 miles, past the old White Chuck River Trail junction (~3,850 ft), to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft beside Sitkum Creek. There, leave the maintained trail on the unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path (closer to a rough angler's path than a real trail), which goes straight up the forested ridge south of Sitkum Creek to Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather and rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. The old approach up the White Chuck River Trail past Kennedy Hot Springs to the same PCT junction is no longer usable: the White Chuck Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7, and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the October 2003 flood. Going out, the PCT climbs back up the valley and over Red Pass before the long descent to the car.
descent: Reverse the route to Boulder Basin camp and the long trail out.

bivy.name: Boulder Basin
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a forested ridge with a full pack. It sits at the end of a long approach from the North Fork Sauk trailhead, over Red Pass and down the upper White Chuck valley on the PCT, so plan the walk in as a trip of its own.
bivy.water: Waterfalls and snowmelt streams run through the basin; dependable into late summer but shrinking as the season goes on. Filter it
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is required for overnight use in this wilderness
bivy.capacity: Several established sites on heather and rock benches at treeline, spread through the basin between roughly 5,500 and 6,000 ft

bivy.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
bivy.notes: Not on the current approach: this site is on the White Chuck River Trail below its junction with the PCT, and that trail has been listed as inaccessible since the 2003 flood. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Parties coming over Red Pass do not pass it.
bivy.water: The river and its tributaries
bivy.capacity: Popular established riverside sites

bivy.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
bivy.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard camp.
bivy.water: Sitkum Creek
bivy.capacity: A small forested site or two just north of the trail junction

days.note: Up North Fork Sauk Trail #649 through old-growth forest and a long set of switchbacks to the Pacific Crest Trail, then north on the PCT over Red Pass into the upper White Chuck valley.
days.title: North Fork Sauk Trail to the PCT and over Red Pass
days.objective: Reach the PCT and cross Red Pass

days.note: Follow the PCT down the upper White Chuck valley to Sitkum Creek, then take the steep, unsigned climbers' path up the ridge south of the creek to the high camp at Boulder Basin.
days.title: Down the PCT to Sitkum Creek and up to Boulder Basin
days.objective: Reach Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft)

days.note: Rope up from Boulder Basin, climb the heavily crevassed Sitkum Glacier to a saddle near Sitkum Spire (~9,500 ft), then follow the pumice/scree ridge (with one short snow traverse) to the summit before reversing back to camp.

schedule.label: Reach the ~9,500 ft saddle
schedule.detail: East of Sitkum Spire, at the top of the glacier.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Final stretch is scree/pumice with a short snow-field traverse.

schedule.label: Back at Boulder Basin camp
schedule.detail: Reverse the glacier; watch for softening snow bridges late in the day.

days.objective: Summit Glacier Peak (10,541 ft) and return to camp

days.note: Break camp, descend the climbers' path to the PCT, and walk back up the White Chuck valley and over Red Pass to the North Fork Sauk Trail and the trailhead.

days.objective: Return to trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day trip at minimum. The walk in from the North Fork Sauk trailhead is far longer than the old White Chuck approach and crosses Red Pass in both directions, so many parties allow an extra day.

name: North Ridge
approach: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on Highway 20 near milepost 163 (roughly 5,100 ft), just east of Washington Pass. From the east end of the pullout, drop into the woods and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path toward Kangaroo Pass. It runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek itself is the common route-finding mistake. Beyond the first mile the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches with intermittent cairns, and the tread all but disappears on the slabs, so route-finding is tricky in fog or fresh snow. It also crosses the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak, a hazard in early season or after new snow. About two miles from the car, cross the last soggy meadow before the path climbs toward Kangaroo Pass and leave it: look up and left (east) for the prominent talus and scree gully that angles back to the deep notch just north of Half Moon. Climb it — a loose slog at the end — to the notch, where the route starts. Water is only reliably available near Early Winters Creek low on the approach; carry what you need above it.
descent: Rappel the North Ridge back to the notch north of the peak, then descend the scree gully and reverse the approach to the highway.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely discouraged rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

itinerary.cal: Approach talus is described as best done with snow cover in early spring, or after it melts out by July, since bare talus is exposed and leg-breaking.

days.note: A long day from the road, no camp: from the hairpin pullout on the highway near Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' path south, staying above Early Winters Creek. About two miles in, cross the last soggy meadow before the path climbs toward Kangaroo Pass and turn up the talus and scree gully that angles back to the deep notch just north of Half Moon. Climb about seven pitches of the North Ridge to the summit, then rappel the route back to the notch and reverse the approach.

name: South Face / Southeast Ridge
approach: From the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR-20 (about 16 miles west of Rainy Pass, elevation ~1,900ft), cross Canyon Creek on a log/plank crossing (can wash out in high water, check current conditions) and follow the Crater Lake/Jackita Ridge Trail (FST 738) as it climbs steeply through forest — roughly 3,400ft of gain in about 4 miles — to the Crater Mountain Trail (FST 746) junction near McMillan Park. Take FST 746 toward Crater Lake (~2,000ft of gain, about 2.3 hours in); this stretch has long, hot, dry switchbacks with no reliable water, so carry what you need from Canyon Creek. Around 6,700–7,200ft, leave the maintained trail and traverse toward the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak (Crater Mountain Saddle, ~7,200ft, roughly 4.2 hours from the trailhead). From the saddle, descend/traverse the Jerry Glacier — often patchy or nearly bare by late summer but still crevassed enough in early season to warrant crampons and a rope — to Jerry Lakes basin (5,900–6,550ft, ~6.4 hours in). From Jerry Lakes, traverse a heather shelf to a 6,520ft notch/pass south of the lakes, then descend about 600ft into Crater Creek Basin through mild terrain and up to the 7,000ft shoulder that accesses the southeast ridge; most parties camp in the 6,000ft basin at Crater Creek Meadows, northwest of point 7,001 (~8.3 hours / roughly 11 miles from the car). On summit day, traverse west from camp across steep scree and dirt slopes below the south face to a landmark 'slinged boulder,' then find a left-slanting ramp that breaches the lower cliff band; a short Class 4 step leads to a hidden Class 3 chimney, above which roughly 1,000ft of Class 2–3 scrambling (with a stretch of exposed low-5th-class climbing and two informal belay stations noted near 8,000ft) gains the southeast ridge and summit block. Hazards throughout: fire-damaged forest sections near Jerry Lakes, loose rock and moats on the glacier margins, crevasse crossings, and significant route-finding difficulty locating the chimney/ramp system on the face.
descent: Reverse the route down the south face and ridge.

bivy.name: Crater Creek Meadows bench
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the standard staging point for the south face, on a heather bench above Crater Creek northwest of point 7001. Reached in roughly eight hours and eleven miles from the car, after the Jerry Glacier traverse and the drop into Crater Creek Basin. Parties choose it over Jerry Lakes specifically because it shortens the summit day onto the face. Terrain gives moderate wind shelter. Permit status is not confirmed for this basin — check the zone before you go.
bivy.water: Crater Creek, about 200 ft below camp
bivy.capacity: small — comfortable for a party of two

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin
bivy.notes: Planned camp, a grassy boulder-strewn bowl with several separate sites; the best of them sits by the small lake between the two large ones. Snow-free by mid-August. It is the more pleasant camp of the two and the obvious stop if you arrive late, but it leaves a longer traverse to the face on summit day. Open bowl, so afternoon wind. Fire-scarred forest on the approach into the basin. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: four alpine lakes
bivy.capacity: multiple parties across the basin

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes Peak south saddle
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — on record only as an unplanned night out, sat through in a bivy sack and an emergency blanket with little wind protection and a cold, sleepless result. Worth knowing exists if a party is caught on the ridge between the lakes and the Crater Mountain saddle, and worth planning not to use.
bivy.water: none at the saddle

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp

itinerary.cal: South Face is typically climbed August-September once snow clears the loose rock; overnight camps fall inside the North Cascades NP Complex/Ross Lake NRA backcountry, which requires a wilderness camping permit.

This is the long day of the trip, mostly off-trail after the saddle.

name: Wilson Glacier Headwall
approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east below Crescent Glacier onto Yakama Nation land, where a separate tribal permit is required and the trail ends at Hellroaring Canyon; the way on, north around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Klickitat and Wilson glacier basins, is a long off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Expect a full day just to reach camp in Avalanche Valley, below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, before a summit attempt.
descent: Descend the South Climb to Cold Springs.

bivy.name: Avalanche Valley
bivy.notes: Meadow basin on the east side of the mountain below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, reached from Bird Creek Meadows or by the Highline Trail. The closest established camp to the Wilson Glacier headwall.
bivy.water: Glacial streams in the valley
bivy.permit: Yakama Nation Tract D permit
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites in a meadow basin

bivy.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
bivy.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends

days.note: The Round the Mountain Trail east from the South Climb trail, then the long, mostly off-trail traverse north round the eastern flank, across the Klickitat Glacier and Big Muddy Creek, to camp in Avalanche Valley below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers.

days.note: An early alpine start from Avalanche Valley, up the Wilson Glacier to the headwall below Roosevelt Cliff (starts around 10,800 ft) — a steep, avalanche/icefall-fed line considered one of Adams' most serious routes. Top out and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs.

name: Buckindy Glacier/Scramble Route
approach: From Darrington, drive north on SR 530 roughly 7-8 miles and turn right onto the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) just after crossing the Sauk River bridge. Follow FR 26 (pavement then gravel) about 20 miles, turn left onto FR 2680, and continue 6 miles to the Green Mountain Trailhead (~3,200 ft). Hike Green Mountain Trail #782 (about 4 miles, ~3,000 ft gain) through old growth and subalpine meadows to the lookout area, then go cross-country along the connecting ridge system east and southeast past the Horse Lake saddle, with slow sidehill travel toward Misch, to Buckindy's north slopes and glacier remnants. This way in has been cut: flood damage closed FR 26 to all motor vehicles at milepost 4, and the closure takes in the Green Mountain Road (FR 2680), which leaves the trailhead roughly twenty miles of closed road past the gate. Check with the Darrington Ranger District before counting on it. The way in that is open comes from the north. Drive Cascade River Road about 14 miles east of Marblemount to Kindy Creek Road (FR 1570), then about 2 miles up that rough spur to a small pullout near 1,850 ft. A climbers' trail climbs Kindy Ridge to a saddle near 4,800 ft south of Point 5116, the same start as for Snowking Mountain. From there, continue south through the Buckindy Range high country to the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages, where parties camp below Buckindy's north side. That ground is a second or third night out.
descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb the Class 4 summit block back onto the glacier, stay roped through the crevassed sections of the Kindy/Goat Creek Glacier, then drop back into the cirque and retrace the approach down Kindy Creek to the FR-1570 pullout off Cascade River Road. Buckindy is also approached from the south over Green Mountain from FR 2680, but that road is closed to vehicles until 2028; parties who come in that way exit that way. The two trailheads are in different drainages roughly 70 road miles apart, so pick one and return to it.

bivy.name: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
bivy.notes: The ground that puts Mount Buckindy in range. Buckindy's standard route is a class 4 scramble on the north slopes, with glaciers on the north and east flanks, and the parties who climb it are camping either in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or at the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages. Coming in from road 1570 this is a second or third night out, well beyond the Cyclone Lake ground. There is a second way in from the south, over Green Mountain and the Horse Lake saddle from the Suiattle side, with camps on the divide and in the basins on the way, but that country has its own long road problems and is not the approach this zone is built around. Nothing here is a site in any developed sense: it is remote, lightly visited ground where the answer to where you sleep is wherever the light runs out, and a party should carry the fuel to melt snow and the tolerance for a dry, windy night.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small basin streams, generally running through midsummer and thinning badly after that. There is ice on Buckindy's north and east flanks, so late in the season the water that is left is glacier outflow rather than clean snowmelt.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on durable ground, pack out human waste, no fires. There is no quota and no reservation anywhere in this zone, so the constraint on a trip here is the approach rather than the paperwork.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on snow, moraine or heather at the passes and in the basins beneath them. Nothing built, no toilet.

bivy.name: Horse Lake saddle camp
bivy.notes: First-night camp on the Green Mountain approach, past the south shoulder of Green Mountain. Beyond it the traverse toward Misch and Buckindy is slow sidehill travel.
bivy.water: Horse Lake and snowmelt nearby; treat it
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites just above the saddle

itinerary.cal: Best conditions are July-September once the approach brush has dried out and the glacier still has manageable snow cover.

days.note: From the FR-1570 pullout walk the brushy, washed-out roadbed almost 2 miles to its end, then climb the steep climbers' trail more than two miles through old growth onto Kindy Ridge and the saddle south of Point 5116, near 4,800 ft. From there the way to Buckindy goes south off trail through the Buckindy Range high country: slow, up-and-down travel that takes most parties two or three days to reach a camp in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek, below Buckindy's north side.
