name: Challenger Glacier
approach: Two approaches are in common use, both starting from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FS Road 32/Ruth Creek Rd off WA-542). Hannegan Pass Trail #674 climbs a well-graded ~2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), the last reliable easy water and the split point for both options. Route A - Whatcom Pass: from the pass, descend a steep, deceptively long ~2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley (Boundary Camp), ford the Chilliwack River (log crossings here are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack), then follow the Chilliwack River Trail up through Copper Creek Camp (reliable water, pit toilet, ~7.5 mi from the trailhead) and on to Whatcom Pass backcountry camp (NPS permit required), roughly 6-7 miles beyond the river crossing. From Whatcom Pass you must get around Whatcom Peak (7,574 ft) to reach Perfect Pass: the North Ridge direct is loose, extremely exposed, 'a formidable obstacle' and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side, which has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses requiring in-and-out crevasse navigation in low-snow years. Route B - Easy Ridge: from the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge (same log-crossing caveat) and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge (site of an old fire lookout), then follow a faint climbers' path along the ridge crest past tarns and slabby sections (mosquito-heavy in season) over Easy Peak to a notch known as 'the Impasse,' continuing cross-country toward Perfect Pass. Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles (matching this route's recorded ~59.5 km distance), so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass and/or Perfect Pass. From Perfect Pass (or the Wiley Lake basin), drop onto the Challenger Glacier at about the 7,000-7,200 ft level - the exact entry point shifts year to year with crevasse conditions - cross a bergschrund, and climb steepening snow (a snow arete in late season) toward the base of the summit rocks. A known late-season hazard just below the summit rocks is a moat that has been reported up to ~5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to find a snow bridge. From Perfect Pass camp itself, getting down onto the glacier can also involve ~200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The final approach to the true summit is a clean 3rd-class scramble to the base of a short (~50 ft), well-protected 5.5-5.7 rock pitch; many parties fix a handline from the summit rappel anchor down to the top of this scramble to manage the exposure on otherwise solid, unbroken rock.
descent: Reverse the glacier; rappel off the summit block

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.notes: The planned high camp for this route and the one everything else is scheduled around. Ground is limited: early in the season much of the pass is still snow-covered and parties either camp on the snow or scout the sandy patches slightly higher on the ridge. It is a pass, so it is windy and weather-exposed with no shelter. Getting from camp onto the glacier is itself part of the climb — depending on melt-out it can mean around 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, so leaving camp in the dark or returning to it late is a real commitment, not a stroll.
bivy.water: Snowmelt at the pass; running water in the gully below it early in the season, drying back as the season goes on, so late-season parties should expect to melt snow
bivy.permit: The Perfect Pass cross-country zone allows exactly one party of up to six per night on a National Park Service backcountry permit, and it is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one. If it is taken, there is no second site here.
bivy.capacity: One party per night, maximum six people — the tightest camp quota in the park's cross-country system

bivy.name: Copper Creek camp
bivy.notes: About 7.5 miles in on the valley approach, with reliable water and a pit toilet. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it exists on this list because the approach to Challenger is long enough that most parties sleep low at least once in each direction. It is also the sensible retreat target if the Chilliwack ford turns you around — the log crossings there are unreliable and have caught parties out.
bivy.water: Copper Creek, reliable
bivy.permit: Designated National Park Service backcountry camp; permit itinerary must name it
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp on the Chilliwack River Trail

bivy.name: Whatcom Pass camp
bivy.notes: The last established camp before the committing ground, used by parties coming in on the Chilliwack River approach. From here you still have to get around Whatcom Peak to reach Perfect Pass — the direct north ridge is loose and very exposed and is not the way most parties go, while the standard workaround crosses the Whatcom Glacier on the peak's east side, which has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years. Treat this as the last comfortable night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and creeks at the pass
bivy.permit: A designated National Park Service backcountry camp; you may only camp in the camp area named on your permit itinerary for the date on it
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites assigned on the permit

itinerary.cal: Best climbed June-Sept once the Chilliwack River ford, the Impasse and the Challenger Glacier are in reasonable shape; the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (used for the Beaver Pass variant) requires advance reservations.

days.note: From the Hannegan Pass trailhead climb about 2,000 ft in 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, drop past Boundary Camp into the Chilliwack valley, and leave the trail where the faint, unsigned climbers' path for Easy Ridge fords the Chilliwack (log crossings here are unreliable). Climb steeply onto Easy Ridge and camp near the tarns on its crest. A long day with a loaded pack: about 8 hours on foot is typical.
days.title: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack to Easy Ridge
days.objective: Camp on the crest of Easy Ridge

days.note: Follow the faint path along the crest over Easy Peak, which has more tent sites and a tarn, to the notch called the Impasse. Where the direct crossing is unsafe, drop off the crest around it and re-climb an exposed class 4 step beyond, then cross the snowfields to Perfect Pass. In fog, keep away from Whatcom Peak's summit wall, which steepens where the pass levels into a saddle.
days.title: Easy Ridge over the Impasse to Perfect Pass
days.objective: Camp at Perfect Pass (about 6,300 ft)

days.note: Get down from Perfect Pass onto the Challenger Glacier (depending on melt-out, about 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat), rope up, cross the bergschrund and climb steepening snow to the summit rocks, watching for the moat below them. A class 3 scramble leads to the 50 ft, 5.5-5.7 summit pitch; rappel it once and reverse the glacier to Perfect Pass. Some parties pack up the same afternoon and recross the Impasse to shorten the walk out.
days.title: Summit day via the Challenger Glacier
days.objective: Climb Mount Challenger via the Challenger Glacier and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach: back along Easy Ridge, down to the Chilliwack ford, and up the long climb to Hannegan Pass before the easy descent to the car.
days.title: Exit to trailhead
days.objective: Hike back out to the Hannegan Pass trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 4-day trip via Easy Ridge (add a spare day for weather), with camps on Easy Ridge and at Perfect Pass and one glacier summit day from Perfect Pass.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River ford / Easy Ridge climbers' path

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft), reached by the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that leaves Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge, follow the Grand Pass Trail along open Lillian Ridge, then down into Grand Valley past Grand and Moose Lakes and up past Gladys Lake to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at about 6 miles. Net gain to the pass is only a few hundred feet, but the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the valley, so total climbing to the pass is close to 2,000 ft. Beyond Grand Pass the trail drops steeply into Cameron Basin, then climbs steeply to Cameron Pass (6,448 ft), the highest trail-served pass in the park; the last part of that climb is loose and rocky in spots and holds snow into midsummer. From Cameron Pass the primitive trail descends into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River and continues to Lost Pass (5,570 ft), the low notch between Lost Peak and Claywood. Parties camp in Upper Cameron Basin or in Lost Basin and climb the peak from there. At Lost Pass leave the trail and head west-southwest across open heather benches and talus toward Claywood, the higher, greyer and more broken summit about a mile and a half away. The final several hundred feet are class 2-3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree, with a short class 3 step on the west side of the summit block. Everything beyond Lost Pass is unmarked and off-trail, so carry a map and GPS and go only in good visibility. Above Lost Pass a workable line climbs steep slopes and light brush to the 6,068 ft bump, then follows a ramp system on the east side of the summit block; it looks too steep from a distance but goes.
descent: Reverse the ascent line back down into the Lost River drainage and up to Cameron Pass, then out via the Cameron Pass and Grand Pass Trails to Obstruction Point. Loose, chossy rock on the upper mountain (typical of this interior Olympic massif) warrants care while downclimbing, especially in descending light or wet conditions.

bivy.name: Dose Meadows
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Claywood, and the southern base for Mount Cameron by way of Lost Pass and Cameron Pass. It sits at about four thousand four hundred and seventy feet at the head of the Dosewallips, and the single fact that dominates any plan built around it is the road. The Dosewallips road has been cut by a washout for over two decades and is not being rebuilt, so you start with roughly five and a half miles of old roadbed before the trail proper, and the meadows are then somewhere around seventeen to nineteen miles from where you actually park. Bicycles are permitted on the roadbed as far as the old ranger station at the wilderness boundary, which removes a meaningful chunk of that and is worth the hassle of hauling a bike. Realistically this is a two-day approach each way for most parties, which puts Claywood firmly in the category of a four to five day objective rather than a weekend. The alternative doors are Gray Wolf Pass from the Gray Wolf river, or the long way round from Obstruction Point, and neither is short. Claywood itself has no established camp of its own: parties climb it from the meadows or bivouac wherever they get to on the ridge, and there is no designated high camp to book.
bivy.water: The infant Dosewallips river runs through the meadows. Reliable.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; not a quota area, so it is normally available. Standard per-permit reservation charge and per-adult nightly fee through the federal recreation booking system, and a hard-sided bear canister is required. There is no permit or fee for the road-walk section below the park boundary, but you do need somewhere legal to leave the car at the closure.
bivy.capacity: Several sites spread through the meadow area, plus stock use in season. It is a junction camp on a long loop, so it is rarely empty and rarely crowded.

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

itinerary.cal: Backcountry permits are required for all overnight stays in Olympic National Park (reserve via the Wilderness Information Center/recreation.gov); snow can linger on Grand Pass and the high cross-country sections into July, so most parties go July–September.

days.note: From Obstruction Point Trailhead, follow the Grand Pass Trail along Lillian Ridge and over Grand Pass, drop into Cameron Basin and climb steeply over Cameron Pass, then descend the primitive trail into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River. Camp is an unmaintained site in Lost Basin (~5,350 ft); the last climb to Cameron Pass is loose and holds snow into midsummer.
days.title: Approach to Lost Basin high camp
days.objective: Reach a rough high camp in Lost Basin below Lost Pass

days.note: Leave the tent at camp and climb steeply to Lost Pass (5,570 ft) between Lost Peak and Claywood, then follow class 2-3 talus and heather slopes west-southwest to the summit before retracing the route back to Lost Basin.
days.title: Summit day: Mount Claywood

schedule.label: Leave Lost Basin camp
schedule.detail: Light day pack; climb toward Lost Pass.

schedule.label: Reach Lost Pass (5,570 ft)
schedule.detail: Col between Lost Peak and Mt Claywood.

schedule.label: Reach the summit scramble
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 talus and heather scrambling begins.

schedule.label: Summit Mount Claywood (6,836 ft)
schedule.detail: Views to Mt Olympus, Mt Cameron, and the Bailey Range.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Retrace the ridge and re-cross Lost Pass.

schedule.label: Back at Lost Basin camp
schedule.detail: Rest, water up, prep for tomorrow's exit.

days.objective: Climb Mount Claywood (6,836 ft) via Lost Pass and return to camp

days.note: Break camp and climb back over Cameron Pass, drop into Cameron Basin, then climb back over Grand Pass before the long descending trail to Obstruction Point. This exit is strenuous in either direction — expect a long, tiring day after two days of off-trail travel.
days.title: Exit via Cameron Pass and Grand Pass
days.objective: Hike out to Obstruction Point Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 3-day, 2-night backpack (about 28 mi round trip, over Grand Pass and Cameron Pass each way) built around one high camp in Lost Basin below Lost Pass — not a car-to-car day trip given how deep and rugged the approach and exit are.

name: Mount Dana Scramble
approach: Getting to the trailhead is part of the approach: flood damage has closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area, and that closure adds about 6.2 miles each way of road walking or biking just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road remains open to foot/bike traffic beyond Madison Falls). From Whiskey Bend, the actual hike-in follows the Elwha River Trail, a well-graded historic path along the river's east bank that passes the old Geyser Valley homestead sites (Michael's Cabin, Humes Ranch) in the first mile or two. The trail is mellow by Olympic standards, staying under roughly 2,000 ft of gain through its first 15+ miles, and passes Lillian River junction (~4 mi), Mary's Falls Camp (8.8 mi), Canyon Camp, Elkhorn Guard Station, and Stony Point as it winds upstream through old-growth forest with the Elwha River itself as a constant, reliable water source. Camp Wilder and Hayes River Guard Station mark roughly the trail's halfway point. Continue up the valley to Chicago Camp, roughly 24-26 trail miles from Whiskey Bend, where the Elwha River must be forded; check conditions before you go, since the crossing can be genuinely hazardous in early-season high water or after rain. At Chicago Camp leave the main trail, which turns south for Low Divide, and take the fainter way trail west up the Elwha toward Elwha Basin, past Happy Hollow camp. Beyond Happy Hollow the route leaves all paths: strike north up the valley side, steep and brushy through timber, to the crest of the ridge that joins Mount Barnes and Mount Wilder. There is no path on the ridge either. Stay high and follow the crest east toward Mount Wilder and then northeast to Dana, finishing with a class 2 scramble to the 6,213-ft summit. Water is scarce once you leave the valley floor, so carry enough for a camp on the ridge. This is a trip of several days, and solid off-trail navigation is essential from Chicago Camp on.

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, Mount Barnes, Mount Noyes and Mount Queets are all short days, Mount Meany is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts Mount Ferry and Mount Pulitzer within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and cross-country zones cannot be booked online — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

itinerary.cal: Requires an Olympic National Park wilderness permit (cross-country nights on the ridge are arranged by phone with the Wilderness Information Center) and is only reasonable snow-free from roughly July through September.

days.note: Walk or ride the closed road from Madison Falls to Whiskey Bend, then follow the Elwha River Trail upstream through old-growth forest past Lillian River, Mary's Falls and Elkhorn. The camps around Hayes River make a sensible first night with a full week's food on your back.
days.title: Madison Falls and Whiskey Bend up the Elwha
days.objective: Camp in the mid-valley, around Hayes River

days.note: Continue up the valley past Camp Wilder to Chicago Camp. The Elwha ford here is the crossing to check before the trip; the main trail turns south for Low Divide, and everything beyond is on the fainter way trail or off-trail.
days.title: Up the Elwha to Chicago Camp
days.objective: Reach Chicago Camp, the last camp on the main trail

days.note: Take the way trail west up the Elwha toward Elwha Basin, past Happy Hollow camp. Beyond it, leave the path and climb north, steeply and through brush and timber, to the crest of the ridge joining Mount Barnes and Mount Wilder. Carry water for the night: the ridge has little.
days.title: Past Happy Hollow and up to the Barnes–Wilder ridge
days.objective: Camp on the ridge between Mount Barnes and Mount Wilder

days.note: With light packs, follow the crest east toward Mount Wilder and on northeast to Dana, finishing with class 2 scrambling to the summit, then return along the ridge to camp. It is a long day for its distance, and Mount Wilder can be taken in on the way back.
days.title: Along the crest to Mount Dana and back
days.objective: Summit Mount Dana (6,213 ft)

days.note: Descend the steep, brushy slope to the Elwha Basin way trail near Happy Hollow, walk back to Chicago Camp, re-ford the Elwha, and continue down the Elwha River Trail to a camp around Hayes River or Elkhorn.
days.title: Down to the valley and back down the Elwha
days.objective: Regain the trail and walk out to the mid-valley camps

days.note: An easy trail walk down the lower Elwha to Whiskey Bend, then the road walk or ride back to Madison Falls.
days.title: Out to Whiskey Bend and Madison Falls
days.objective: Return to the car

itinerary.totalNote: A six-day out-and-back up the Elwha: two days of trail walking to Chicago Camp, a steep off-trail climb from the Elwha Basin way trail to the Barnes–Wilder ridge, a day along the crest to Dana and back, and two days out.

waypoints.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha

name: Standard Route
approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel. In late July the glacier east of Mount Carrie can be skirted along its northwest edge on rock; drop to a tarn near 5,900 ft, hold that height to a gully that rises straight to the ridge, then walk the ridge to the top.
descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
bivy.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a quota camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, quota camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

itinerary.cal: Best from mid-July to early September. Earlier, steep snow can linger on the Catwalk and the Carrie side; later, the glacier runs to bare ice and its snow bridges thin.

days.note: Walk the Sol Duc River Trail past Sol Duc Falls and climb to the High Divide by way of Deer Lake or Heart Lake, then follow the divide east to the Cat Basin junction, where the maintained trail ends. Fill every bottle before leaving the divide trail: the way on toward Cat Peak carries no water. Camp in Cat Basin, the last sheltered ground before the route goes cross-country.
days.title: Sol Duc trailhead to Cat Basin
days.objective: Camp in Cat Basin below Cat Peak

days.note: Leave Cat Basin on the boot path below Cat Peak and cross the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed ridge between Cat Peak and Mount Carrie. With a full pack it is the crux of the approach, and no place to be in wet weather. Camp at Boston Charlie's on the far side, where the only water is a small sinkhole pond that must be filtered.
days.title: Across the Catwalk to Boston Charlie's
days.objective: Camp at Boston Charlie's, at the foot of Mount Carrie

days.note: Climb roughly 2,000 ft from camp to the summit of Mount Carrie. From Carrie's top, rope up and put on crampons, head northeast down onto the glacier, circle round to the north side of Fairchild and climb its Southwest Ridge to the summit. Reverse the whole line back over Carrie to camp, allowing for snow bridges that soften through the afternoon.
days.title: Summit day: over Mount Carrie to Fairchild
days.objective: Summit Mount Fairchild (6,899 ft) and return to Boston Charlie's

days.note: Recross the Catwalk to Cat Basin, regain the High Divide trail and follow it back down past Sol Duc Falls to the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out to Sol Duc
days.objective: Return to the Sol Duc trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 4-day, 3-night out-and-back from the Sol Duc trailhead: a trail day to Cat Basin, a short day across the Catwalk to Boston Charlie's, a long summit day over Mount Carrie to Fairchild and back, and a long day out.

name: West Face
approach: Drive the paved Upper Hoh Road to its end at the Hoh Ranger Station (578 ft). Hike the Hoh River Trail 17.2 miles to Glacier Meadows (~4,200-4,300 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the range (note: a washed-out section partway up requires a fixed ladder/rope crossing). From Glacier Meadows, follow the way trail 0.8 mi to the top of the Blue Glacier lateral moraine, continue along the moraine crest ~0.2 mi, then descend onto the Blue Glacier and ascend snow slopes around rock islands to the crest of Snow Dome (6,600 ft). From Snow Dome, rope up and continue up the upper Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass (the saddle between Mathias and the East Peak of Olympus, at the head of the Hoh Glacier), then gain the base of either the Mathias snow finger or the steep gullies leading to the Mercury-Mathias col.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows
bivy.notes: The standard base camp for climbs off the Blue Glacier, about 17 miles up the Hoh River Trail. Summit day starts with the short way trail to the Blue Glacier moraine.
bivy.water: Creek beside camp
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: Several designated tent sites in the forest at the end of the Hoh River Trail

bivy.name: Snow Dome high camp
bivy.notes: Higher option on the rocks of the lower Snow Dome or on its crest, above the Blue Glacier. It shortens the day to Glacier Pass and Mathias; carry out human waste.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few rock-sheltered tent sites on and below the crest of the Snow Dome

itinerary.cal: Needs an Olympic National Park wilderness permit for the nights at Glacier Meadows. The route is in condition roughly July to September, and it goes faster and more safely while the snow finger still holds snow rather than bare ice or scree.

days.note: The long, mostly gentle Hoh River Trail through the rainforest, climbing steadily only in the last few miles out of the valley. A washed-out section near the top is crossed on a fixed ladder. Packs carry full glacier kit.
days.title: Hoh trailhead to Glacier Meadows
days.objective: Reach the Glacier Meadows base camp

days.note: Take the way trail to the Blue Glacier moraine, rope up and cross the glacier to Snow Dome, then continue up the upper Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass, the saddle between Mathias and the East Peak of Mount Olympus. Climb the steep snow finger between Mathias and the pass, or the gullies to the Mercury-Mathias col, to Class 4 rock on the summit ridge. Reverse the climb and recross the glacier to Glacier Meadows. Mount Mercury is often added from the col.
days.title: Blue Glacier, Glacier Pass and the Mathias summit
days.objective: Climb Mount Mathias by the snow finger or the Mercury-Mathias col and return to camp

days.note: A long, mostly downhill trail day back to the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Walk back down the Hoh River Trail to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: An out-and-back from the Hoh: a long trail day in to Glacier Meadows, a roped glacier day to Glacier Pass and the summit ridge, and the walk out. Many parties add a spare day for weather or climb Mathias alongside Mount Olympus.

waypoints.name: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)

name: South Slopes (Standard)
approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, 16 miles one-way by the river trail and much farther by the ridge, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it is closed to vehicles at Madison Falls by a washout, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach, up from the North Fork Quinault side, follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
descent: Reverse the south slopes to Seattle Meadows, then descend to Low Divide and the North Fork Quinault trail.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

itinerary.cal: Olympic National Park wilderness permits (quota-based in summer) are required for all backcountry camps along this route; check current park conditions for the North Fork Quinault fords, especially the Sixteen Mile crossing, before committing to the approach.

days.note: From the North Fork Quinault trailhead at road's end, the trail follows the valley floor through old-growth forest past Wolf Bar and Halfway House. Wild Rose Creek and Elip Creek are fords that can run fast in heavy rain or peak snowmelt. Full packs, modest grade — this is mileage-banking, not climbing.
days.title: Up the North Fork Quinault River Trail
days.objective: Reach a river camp such as Elip Creek or Sixteen Mile

days.note: Ford the North Fork at Sixteen Mile (normally knee- to thigh-deep and swift, and hazardous or impassable in heavy rain or snowmelt), then make the steep, loose climb to Low Divide (3,602 ft), the pass between the Quinault and Elwha drainages. Continue into Seattle Creek Basin and up to a meadow camp near 4,550 ft at Seattle Meadows, below the peak's west slopes.
days.title: Over the Sixteen Mile ford to Low Divide and high camp
days.objective: Reach a high camp at Seattle Meadows

days.note: Leave the tent at camp and go light. Climb scree on the peak's western side, cross over the ridge and ascend talus on the eastern side to the east ridge, then Class 2-3 scrambling to the 6,246 ft summit; reverse the same line back to camp.
days.title: Summit day

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Light daypack; rope/overnight gear left at camp.

schedule.label: Gain the south/east ridge
schedule.detail: Talus and scree slopes above Seattle Meadows basin.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 scramble; views across the Bailey Range and Elwha headwaters.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the south-side scree/talus line.

schedule.label: Back at high camp
schedule.detail: Rest of the day free to recover before the long walk out begins.

days.objective: Climb Mount Seattle via the south-side talus/scree slopes

days.note: Drop back to Low Divide, descend the steep trail to the Sixteen Mile ford and continue down the North Fork valley as far as is reasonable with a full pack after a summit day.
days.title: Back down to the North Fork
days.objective: Return to a river camp below Low Divide

days.note: Finish down the North Fork Quinault valley to the cars, re-crossing the Elip Creek and Wild Rose Creek fords. A long but easy-grade final day.
days.title: Hike out to the trailhead
days.objective: Return to the North Fork Quinault trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A multi-day wilderness backpack (about 5 days / 4 nights) up the North Fork Quinault River, 16 trail miles to Low Divide, then on to a high camp at Seattle Meadows, with a half-day scramble to the 6,246 ft summit and the same trail back out.

waypoints.name: North Fork Quinault Trailhead (North Shore Road)
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha

name: Southwest Ridge
approach: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR 34), and follow FR 34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (do not confuse with the separate Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR 32). Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge, and early-summer high water can make it difficult or unsafe to cross. Follow the old roadbed/Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west/southwest ridge, passing through/around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system. Above the cliff band, the summit gully splits into several forks; the leftmost fork (or the one just west of a snow couloir to its right) is easiest, and rock is generally solid low but looser near the summit ridge. Note a separate, lower-angle north-side line — via Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier to the SE ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed ~100 ft Class 3 traverse, and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak; don't confuse the two lines when planning.
descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

itinerary.cal: Climbed June-September when Ruth Creek is fordable; snow may linger in the gully early season (axe/crampons useful), while late season favors a low, easy creek crossing but thicker brush.

days.note: A long single-day outing: ford Ruth Creek, follow the old logging roadbed, then leave the trail for a brushy ascending traverse onto Sefrit's southwest ridge past a cliff band. Climb Class 4 rock into the upper gully system, taking the easiest (leftmost) fork to the summit ridge, then reverse the whole route to descend. Routefinding and brush in the approach/traverse are the main time sink, not the climbing itself.
days.title: Car-to-car climb

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Ford Ruth Creek at the end of FR 34 (log crossing possible in low water); most parties start pre-dawn given the length of the day.

schedule.label: Reach end of old roadbed
schedule.detail: Old logging roadbed gives easy walking before the trail runs out.

schedule.label: Ascending traverse to the ridge
schedule.detail: Leave the trail, thrash through brush/slide alder past a cliff band onto the west/southwest ridge proper - the slowest, most routefinding-dependent stretch of the day.

schedule.label: Class 4 gully system
schedule.detail: Enter the gully and take the easiest upper fork (leftmost, west of the snow couloir); one steep-but-clean Class 4 step is the technical crux.

schedule.label: Summit (7,191 ft)
schedule.detail: Cairned summit; views of Mt. Shuksan's north face and the Nooksack Cirque.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Descend by reversing the ascent; some parties rappel the Class 4 step from a large block on the SW side rather than downclimbing it.

days.objective: Summit via the SW ridge/gully system and return to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day car-to-car: roughly 10-14 hours, ~5,000 ft gain - no camp, done entirely in a day like the other standard routes on this peak.

name: Mount Olympus Traverse (West–Middle–East Peaks)
approach: Same Hoh River Trail (17.4 mi) and Blue Glacier approach to Glacier Meadows as the standard route (5-Mile Island, Olympus Guard Station/High Hoh Bridge, Lewis Meadow ~11 mi as the common overnight, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows at 4,300 ft), then the ~1-mi lateral-moraine crossing onto the glacier. From Snow Dome (~6,600–6,800 ft), the traverse follows the standard Crystal Pass line — over Crystal Pass, south of (below) Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit — to the West Peak (7,980 ft), then continues east across intervening terrain to the Middle Peak (7,929 ft) and finally the East Peak (7,762 ft). This is a multi-day, largely off-trail glacier and ridge outing; expect sustained glacier travel with crevasse and icefall exposure the entire way, and carry a full rescue kit for the whole traverse, not just the West Peak summit pitch.
descent: From the East Peak, descend to Glacier Meadows via Glacier Pass.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, quota-limited, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

bivy.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
bivy.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is glacier camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
bivy.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

itinerary.cal: Glacier Pass has reported icefall hazard and deep snow moats near Middle Peak in recent seasons; conditions vary enough year to year that some parties substitute easier Panic Peak for East Peak.

days.note: Flat old-growth valley approach along the Hoh River.
days.title: Hoh River Trail to Olympus Guard Station
days.objective: Reach Lewis Meadow / Olympus Guard Station camp

days.note: A long linkup day: climb the West Peak via the standard Blue Glacier/Snow Dome/Crystal Pass line, descend and re-ascend to Middle Peak, continue to East Peak, then descend to Glacier Meadows via Glacier Pass. Deep moats and icefall hazard near Glacier Pass are commonly reported.

itinerary.totalNote: A 5-day trip: 2 days up to Glacier Meadows, one very long day linking West, Middle and East peaks via Glacier Pass, a built-in buffer day, and a day to hike out — matching the advice to plan an extra day versus the standard single-summit climb.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: No trail reaches Rimrock Ridge. The way in is the north end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road and climb the Cascade Pass trail, then follow the traverse's climbers' path over Cache Col and down to Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. The next day crosses the exposed Red Ledge below Arts Knoll and the crevassed Middle Cascade Glacier (rope up) to the Spider–Formidable col, then drops to Yang Yang Lakes, the usual second camp. On the third day the traverse climbs back to the Le Conte ridge and up the Le Conte Glacier to the col between Le Conte and Sentinel at its head. The parties on record left the traverse here, passed north of Sentinel Peak and followed the ridge east along its crest; the ridge is the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek. Beyond the traverse the line is cross-country alpine ground with no path, and no detailed description of it is published. The Agnes Creek trail (PCT) from High Bridge runs up a different valley and does not lead to the ridge.

itinerary.totalNote: Three days on the Ptarmigan Traverse reach the col between Le Conte and Sentinel, where the line onto Rimrock Ridge begins. No published account gives a schedule for the ridge itself or for leaving it, so no total length is stated here.
